item.title: I compared 4K Blu-ray to regular Blu-ray, and the difference was smaller than I expected
item.itunes:title: I compared 4K Blu-ray to regular Blu-ray, and the difference was smaller than I expected
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently ran a test comparing an upscaled DVD on my Nvidia Shield to 4K streaming, and the results were intriguing. It was a closer contest than I expected; I knew I couldn't watch streaming without seeing compression artifacts. When it comes to media, we want the best quality possible.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But I don't assume something is better just because we're told it is. So, I was curious about the quality and price difference between a UHD 4K and a standard (non-upscaled) Blu-ray disc. Is the difference big enough to justify $10-15 more per disc and gigs of server space?

Creating a uniform comparison

Same movie, TV, and Blu-ray player setting adjustments

I chose a movie from the MCU because it has spectacular visuals, color, and detail. I picked Spider-Man: Far From Home since I've seen it enough times to know what to look for in key scenes. I played both discs on the same Panasonic DP-UB820 UHD Blu-ray player through a Vizio 4K TV. I also kept the same TV settings to avoid skewing my anecdotal test. I restored the TV's settings to default and used the TV's default calibrated dark setting with no other picture adjustments.

Another issue I had to address is that my Blu-ray player upscales standard Blu-ray discs to 4K by default, which is a nice feature, but not for this test. So I went into its settings and changed the resolution from 4K to 1080p. I switched the player's output to standard Blu-ray and left the TV to handle scaling to fit the 3840×2160 pixel resolution display. I wanted to ensure I was getting the full visual experience of the 1080p Blu-ray without upscaling getting in the way.

I did this test with the actual discs and not Blu-ray rips. I wanted to ensure I was using the full amount of data each disc contains to compare picture and sound quality. Even a properly ripped MakeMKV Blu-ray remux copies the disc's audio and video without re-encoding, but server and network issues can still affect quality. Transcoding, tone-mapping, and network issues can affect playback. Using physical discs, the same player and TV kept the playback devices consistent without introducing media servers.

I thought all Blu-ray drives were the same until I found the perfect one for ripping physical media to Plex

All Blu-ray drives aren't created equal when you're backing up 4K movies for self-hosted media servers.

By  Brian Burgess

Regular Blu-ray looks great

The movie on the disc was impressive

After adjusting my player's settings, I watched the full movie starting on the standard Blu-ray at its native resolution. It looked good. For a Marvel flick, the colors popped, scenes were clean and tight, and the movie was enjoyable. It certainly didn't have grainy DVD quality. I wasn't thinking about what I might be missing, and I never felt the urge to pop in the 4K UHD disc while I watched.

Overall, nothing about the picture irked me. If I weren't doing this comparison, I would have been satisfied with the regular Blu-ray version without thinking about resolution at all. In fact, if I was watching the movie on the screen, it would have been satisfying because I was absorbed in the story. I wouldn't have known it was lower resolution than 4K. Details were clear in the scenes; nothing looked muddy, noticeably off, or hard to distinguish. I couldn't pick out anything wrong like I can on so-called 4K streaming.

Testing the UHD 4K disc

From HD to ultra-HD wasn't a huge difference

After adjusting my player's settings, I watched the full movie starting on the standard Blu-ray at its native resolution. It looked good. For a Marvel flick, the colors popped, scenes were clean and tight, and the movie was enjoyable. It certainly didn't have grainy DVD quality. I wasn't thinking about what I might be missing, and I never felt the urge to pop in the 4K UHD disc while I watched.

Overall, nothing about the picture irked me. If I wasn't doing this comparison, I would have been satisfied with the regular Blu-ray version without thinking about resolution at all. In fact, if I was just walking by the screen to watch the movie, it would have been satisfying since I was absorbed in the story. I wouldn't have known it was lower resolution than 4K. Details were clear in the scenes; nothing looked muddy, noticeably off, or hard to distinguish. I couldn't pick out anything wrong like I can on so-called 4K streaming.

Every time a movie disappears from streaming, I'm glad I already own it on Blu-ray

Owning physical media can't be emphasized enough in a streaming age where movies vanish.

1
By  Brian Burgess

The 4K Blu-ray looked better, but a standard Blu-ray is no slouch

It wasn't a way better experience in 4K

When I popped in the UHD 4K disc after watching the standard Blu-ray version, I was expecting it to look better, and it did. However, it wasn't a magical new experience that made me never want to watch a 1080p disc again. I remember the jump from DVD to Blu-ray, and it was a major contrast in quality. A standard Blu-ray already displays detailed textures, colors, and clear images, which gives UHD something to build on. But the quality difference between standard Blu-ray and UHD isn't there.

Not all standard Blu-ray discs look as good as my Spider-Man — the source material, mastering, and compression by studios and production partners matter. Blu-ray.com gave this disc a five-star rating for audio and video. Still, it's worth comparing versions to see whether a standard disc is good enough. I'm glad I did this test and found that, at least for modern movies, it might be enough.

Many of my UHD Blu-ray discs include the standard Blu-ray. I'm going to do more comparisons, and potentially start saving much-needed storage space on my media servers. I can rip the Blu-ray and replace the 4K files. I will need to see how standard Blu-ray rips perform, but if they hold up, I can start saving on storage. I won't go as far as only buying standard Blu-ray. But if I can spend less on server storage and keep my library, it's a win.

I automated my Blu-ray ripping setup, and now building my movie library costs next to nothing

I don't need to break the bank for storage

5
By  Jasmine Mannan

Standard Blu-ray is great, and a cheaper solution in many ways

If you don't have a super high-resolution TV set, a standard Blu-ray looks great. Unless you're a videophile, even on a TV with incredible resolution, you won't notice the difference until you watch the versions back-to-back. The bottom line is a modern, properly transferred standard Blu-ray is great, but 4K does look better. But it isn't as impressive as the leap from DVD to Blu-ray.

Now, I'm rethinking how I rip and replace files in my media library. Or at least re-encode 4K rips. I'm not going all in on standard Blu-ray. Future-proof media and having choice is nice. But storage is at a premium, and prices aren't going down anytime soon.

item.title: I stopped copying ISOs to my Ventoy drive because this free tool lets me boot operating systems over the network
item.itunes:title: I stopped copying ISOs to my Ventoy drive because this free tool lets me boot operating systems over the network
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I frequently install operating systems, which means downloading the latest ISO files. Whether it's Windows, a Linux distribution, or a tool, you first need to download it and then write it to a USB drive. Rufus is a great tool to do so, but recreating a bootable USB drive is tedious. Ventoy lets you keep multiple ISO files for any OS or tool on a single bootable USB drive. I have one such drive with ten useful tools and ISO files of my commonly used operating systems.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But even USB drives or an SSD have a fixed storage space. You cannot just copy everything onto it and only have to keep the most necessary ones. I recently tried a tool that doesn't force you to download an ISO file beforehand to install the OS. It handles everything and makes me question the future of my Ventoy USB.

Ventoy is a great tool

But you can't put everything on one drive

My Ventoy drive has 28GB of available storage space, and Ubuntu, Windows 11, Windows 10, and two MX Linux distributions occupy most of it. I could use a bigger drive, but that won't get me the distro variety I need when I want to install on someone else's system. Ventoy can even run from an SSD, but in this expensive storage era, you have to be mindful.

I would prefer using the SSD for something more useful. It can serve as an OS installation drive rather than storing a bunch of ISO files. ISO files can also become outdated, and you have to download newer versions when they are released. So, what's the alternative? Network boot.

My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use

My full setup, wherever I go

12
By  João Carrasqueira

The concept has been around for a while, and I use netboot.xyz. It uses iPXE to connect to its own server, from which it can fetch installers, live environments, and a few more resources for multiple operating systems. So your Ventoy drives stay lean, and you only need one tool to install multiple OS and their variants.

Netboot.xyz has a diverse range of options

Moderate setup complexity

Whenever you think of a network-based tool with no graphical interface, you question how easy it is to use. I was also skeptical of using it because when you load such tools, they need to identify your installed hardware. You can create a dedicated USB drive for netboot.xyz, but I prefer keeping it on the Ventoy drive instead. I can simply plug in the Ventoy drive, load its GUI interface, and then navigate to the CLI version of this tool.

Once you load the netboot.xyz’s interface, you need to configure the network connection. I thought it would pick up Ethernet effortlessly, but I didn't have success with it. So, I had to manually set up the connection with all the details, like IP address, subnet mask, DNS, and gateway, to make the connection usable. Only then did the tool’s interface load the necessary options, including the ability to boot from a local drive.

I use Rescuezilla to swap between operating systems and I love it

Distro hopping just got a lot easier.

12
By  Simon Batt

It divides the page into four categories. The first is booting from the local HDD, which takes you directly to the currently installed OS. Next is the distribution category, which lists Linux distributions, Live CDs, BSD, Unix network installs, FreeDOS, and Windows. I mostly deal with Linux distributions and use that option because it lists a range of options. There are two dozen Linux distributions to choose from, including the popular ones like Debian, Fedora, Kali Linux, and a lot more.

But that’s not all! Netboot.xyz understands that ISOs are not enough, and you need to have a few tools as well. GParted, MemTest86+, Clonezilla, and ShredOS are tools that must be on any rescue USB. In fact, I have most of the tools listed on its list on my Ventoy drive, and their ISO files take up a lot of storage space. As a result, I’ve deleted all the common ones from my Ventoy drive and only keep Hiren’s BootCD PE on the Ventoy drive.

Seamless OS installations

Network speed plays a crucial role

I installed many distros using netboot.xyz, and it takes a bit longer to complete than your standard installation. Since it has to fetch the files and additional resources from multiple repositories and then copy them to your machine, your internet speed plays an important role. You might not notice it while installing something as small as Tiny Core Linux. I installed Debian, and it took around 45 minutes to complete on a virtual machine.

I also tested the same installation on an old laptop with an HDD and Ethernet connections, and the results were similar. The tool can work with 1GB or more of memory. However, its official page also mentions that the requirement can exceed 4GB for some rescue environments with a GUI. I mostly stick to the Linux distribution options. You have to add a download URL to install Windows, which is a bit inconvenient.

Ventoy made testing operating systems a breeze

It's a whole new world

6
By  João Carrasqueira

Instead, I prefer keeping Windows 11 and 10 and the MX Linux ISO on the Ventoy drive, and use netboot.xyz mostly for mainstream distros like Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora. This approach saves quite a bit of storage space that was previously occupied by tools and Linux ISOs. My main reason for keeping one Linux ISO is to mitigate network problems. In case of a network outage or misconfiguration, I can still use some troubleshooting tools included with most Linux distros.

Reduce the load on your Ventoy drive

I finally have a tool that can help me keep the Ventoy drive free for other things like live persistence. Netboot.xyz covers a diverse range of tools and ISOs and is very easy to use once you set up a proper network connection. Memory isn't an issue when installing most of the distros or tools listed. You can even host your personal iPXE server with netboot.xyz locally and keep a copy of a few distros on it. I prefer downloading ISOs from its sources because they are the latest versions.

Netboot.xyz

Netboot is a PXE server that lives in the cloud.

item.title: I gave Claude, ChatGPT, and a local 9B model the same 20 tasks, and only one was worth paying for
item.itunes:title: I gave Claude, ChatGPT, and a local 9B model the same 20 tasks, and only one was worth paying for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As we head into 2027, Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT both make a convincing case for a subscription. I personally use ChatGPT more because I can get more done within its usage limits than I can with Claude. But if you’re a tinkerer like me with a local model running on your computer, you also have to ask whether you need to pay for either.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I gave Claude, ChatGPT, and the Qwen3.5-9B model running through LM Studio the same 20 tasks I regularly do, including coding, troubleshooting, and automation. I compared the responses for accuracy, how much I could actually use, and how much guidance each needed to finish the task. I wanted to know which subscription earned its place, and whether the free local option could save me the expense.

I started with the everyday requests

Small tasks gave me a baseline

I use AI for plenty of small jobs when I’m tinkering with my self-hosted setup. I regularly ask it to explain a configuration setting, help me understand an error, or generate a short function for something I’m building. These requests make up a useful part of my everyday AI use, so I included them in the comparison. I wanted to see how much the models differed on work that shouldn’t require extensive reasoning or a long conversation.

For coding, I started with requests where I could describe exactly what I needed. Giving the local model a function’s inputs, expected output, and any constraints gives it a reasonable chance of producing useful code. It also handles general technical questions and explanations of short code snippets. I still need to check its answers, but keeping the scope small makes that manageable.

The difficulty increases when I ask it to make decisions about a larger task. If I want to add a feature, I get further by breaking it into individual changes and asking the model to handle each one separately. That works, although I’m doing much of the planning myself. I have to decide what information it needs, supply that information, and check whether each change fits the rest of the project.

ChatGPT gives me useful help with less of that preparation, even on its free tier. Claude also handles these smaller requests well, although they give me fewer reasons to pay than the more demanding work does. The local model gets enough right to remain useful for narrow questions and small coding jobs.

I've spent over $3,000 on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and only one was worth the money

$3,000 later, I've finally learned my lesson

6
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Claude pulled ahead on the bigger jobs

Following through takes more than code

Most of the projects I use AI for involve changing something that already exists. If I need to use AI to add a feature to an app, it needs to understand the current code, find the relevant files, and make changes that work together. If something breaks, the model should be able to investigate the problem and continue.

I’ve used Claude Code to build a shared grocery app for my family, with sign-in, a shared list, and reminders. That kind of project involves enough connected decisions that checking individual code snippets only tells me so much. I need help carrying a feature through the app and getting it working. Claude gives me the most usable assistance with that work, and I spend less time correcting its approach.

The same applies when I give the model access to tools. You can connect an MCP server to make its tools available, but the model still has to choose the right tool, supply the right arguments, and understand the result. Browsing adds another layer – it needs to find relevant information and use it to complete the request. I get the most consistent results from Claude across these longer sequences. My local 9B model struggles so much with them that I can’t rely on it to carry the task through.

ChatGPT is also useful for these tasks, and I still use it for a lot of technical work. In my experience, Claude's advantage is how directly its help translates into progress. With the local model, I spend too much time supervising decisions and checking whether it has actually accomplished what I asked.

The tasks made the differences clearer

Claude needed less help to finish

To get into the details of which model performed better across the tasks, let’s look at five examples that show where the differences became most obvious. I started with a Python function that I needed to process analytics data. Claude and ChatGPT easily handled the request. The local 9B model also produced usable code, although I had to correct its course multiple times.

Next, I asked them to help troubleshoot a Docker container that wouldn’t start. Claude gave me the clearest direction for investigating the configuration and logs. ChatGPT provided equally useful troubleshooting help. The local model could explain individual errors, but needed a lot of handholding and often gave outdated instructions and commands.

For the app-development task, I asked them to help add a feature to my family’s grocery app. Claude handled the connected changes most effectively and needed fewer corrections. ChatGPT remained useful for implementation and debugging. With the local model, I had to break the feature into smaller changes and take responsibility for how they fit together.

I also included an n8n workflow for identifying emails that needed a reply. Claude gave me the most usable JSON for connecting the steps and troubleshooting the workflow. ChatGPT also handled the logic competently. The local model couldn’t do the full workflow, although checking individual messages against predefined criteria remained a more realistic job for it.

Finally, I asked them to research a self-hosted app using its current documentation. Claude and ChatGPT made much better use of browsing tools. The local model needed considerably more supervision to find and use the information, which reduced the benefit of handing it the task.

Claude earns the subscription for me

Claude’s tighter usage limits frustrate me, and I still reach for ChatGPT more often. But when I need help finishing a complicated project, Claude gives me usable results with fewer corrections. That’s enough to justify the subscription for me, even with a free local model sitting on my computer.

I run OpenCode with a different model for every job, and I haven't hit a rate limit yet

I stopped leaning on one model for everything

item.title: Windows has been sending every Start menu search to Bing for over a decade, and one new toggle fixes it
item.itunes:title: Windows has been sending every Start menu search to Bing for over a decade, and one new toggle fixes it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
No one looks at Windows Search and thinks that it would be a great search engine. I'd even go so far to say that most people on Windows 11 don't think of it as one at all, because, after all, it's a box where you expect to type the name of a folder, app, or image you've been looking for and be able to open it right away.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

And yet, for the longest time, Windows Search had a notorious tendency to pass whatever you typed in to Bing and offer to search the web for a file you already had on your C: drive. In late August, however, Microsoft finally started rolling out a toggle that turns off this pointless quirk for good. I tested it with Sysinternals TCPView after flipping it, and I can finally rest assured knowing that all my searches pull results from my own PC instead of Bing as they're supposed to.

Windows Search phoned Microsoft every time I typed something

My own files came second, and that's not a great experience

I've recently updated to Windows 11 26H2, and I've spoken about how the enablement package has unlocked the right settings and toggles for users. When a toggle to finally turn off web results showed up in Settings, I wanted to know whether it fully stopped Search from talking to Bing or just hid the results.

So, to test it, before flipping the switch, I opened Sysinternals TCPView beside the search panel and used a short PowerShell script to tie the WebView2 process drawing the results to SearchHost, which is the process behind Search.

As I had expected, fresh connections appeared under that process instantaneously while I was still typing, almost all to Microsoft-owned addresses, including one to the same server range that serves Bing's website on my network.

I ran a few keywords that led me to a web search as the best match, with some results offering five more web suggestions, an AI Overview card, and a button to open it all in Edge. That was enough to establish that every one of those results had to travel to Microsoft and back before Search could show it.

Windows search can be a drag. For a better search experience, check out Everything from Voidtools.

2
By  Brian Burgess

How I finally turned web search off on Windows Search

To their credit, Microsoft has made it really easy to do it

Amongst the various deficiencies of Windows Search, the one I would argue hurts the user experience the most is being redirected to a search engine when I search for a file that's already on my drive.

It's one of the most frequently cited reasons as to why users moved to third-party alternatives on the OS. As such, I'd say that this "fix" from Microsoft was amongst the most awaited ones, and it is indeed fortunate that it makes it so easy to toggle.

The first thing I had to do was to go into Settings and from there, Privacy & Security to access the settings surrounding Search.

From there, I had to click Search which took me to a page listing my indexing status, and just below it, a section called "Show suggested search results." Expanding it revealed two toggles, one for Web searches and one for Microsoft Store. I turned off Web searches although, it's nice to see an option that keeps the Microsoft Store suggestions out of my results as well.

If you're trying to go through these steps and don't see the option to do so, the first thing to do is to check and update your OS to the latest version. The feature is a part of 26H2, which is now available to every eligible PC running 24H2 or 25H2. Microsoft is rolling it out in stages, though, so there's a chance that even an up-to-date PC might be missing it at the moment.

Microsoft is finally tidying up the Search options in the Windows 11 Settings page

It has a new visual makeover, too.

By  Simon Batt

It took one toggle to shut up Bing for good

"No results found" never looked better in a search result

I ran the same test again with the Web search off with TCPView open beside the search panel. Refreshingly enough, typing didn't spawn a new connection under the Search process. A later run did show a few new connections, though, so the toggle keeps Bing out of your search results rather than taking Search fully offline.

Additionally, I also ran a few other search items, including those matching file names on my system and those that had no corresponding file names. Those without corresponding file names returned a rather satisfactory "No results found" (which, I must admit, I'd seen for the first time on Windows Search). Also worth noting that even the Web tab disappeared from the filters at the top.

Search is finally becoming what it should've been from day one

It only took Microsoft a decade to fix it, but Windows Search feels like it's finally doing what it's intended to do, which is, to search my local files on my PC without offering a detour to the Edge web browser.

The fix to this problem has arrived as a singular toggle which will take a few seconds to enable, but my user experience on Windows 11 will benefit from it for as long as I stick to the platform. For those who have been sticking to third-party alternatives for searching for files on the OS, this one feature might make it worth coming back to the native search.

item.title: I built a Linux command alias system that handles my entire workflow, and now I type two characters instead of thirty
item.itunes:title: I built a Linux command alias system that handles my entire workflow, and now I type two characters instead of thirty
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For a long time, most of my edits to .bashrc were small shortcuts for switches I used constantly and didn't want to type every time, like ls -la. It also contained a handful of git aliases and some chained commands that I'd turned into functions. These were nice to have, and I mistakenly thought that was nearly all the convenience I'd be able to extract from making aliases.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The main thing that was holding me back from creating more aliases was that a lot of the routine work I do can't benefit from shortcuts that just point to static commands. Sometimes I need to do things in a specific order, or a command needs to take certain arguments that vary between runs.

I finally addressed that problem by tying everything in my alias system to functions. Now, I can access any of them with the same two-letter command, kb, which I named after my own initials simply because it's fast to type and impossible to forget.

Aliases are only useful to a certain point

Functions are better when you need to add logic

Aliases come in handy, but they're extremely simple. All they really are is string substitution. A common one that almost everyone knows is ll, which the shell expands to ls -la before running the command. It's great for saving a few keystrokes, but not that useful when you need to add something, like a condition or argument, that changes the behavior.

Functions, on the other hand, are like mini Bash scripts that allow us to insert logic into a command or sequence of commands. They're dynamic because calling them from different directories or under different conditions can change the result. My project launcher is a good example of this:

proj() {
  cd ~/dev/"$1" && source venv/bin/activate && tmux new -s "$1"
}

I can't tell you how many times I manually typed out each of those commands before I finally put them in a function. Now all I need to do is type proj and one argument (budget, in this case) to change directory to the right project, activate its virtual environment, and open a new tmux session under the same name.

At this point, I've accumulated a few dozen functions just like that which cover all the most common parts of my workflow. I have one for backups, file transfers, SSHing into different hosts, and even one to download a video from YouTube, among many others. I keep all my custom aliases and functions in a separate .bash_shortcuts file, which I source at the top of .bashrc. I find that it keeps everything more portable and organized that way.

A dispatcher helped me clean up my aliases

Now it doesn't matter if I forgot what I named something

The problem with having more than 40 aliases and functions is that I inevitably forget what I named some of them. That's especially true for the handful that I only use every couple of weeks. The solution to that problem is my two-letter dispatcher, which routes arguments through a case statement like this:

kb() {
  case "$1" in
    deploy) ./deploy.sh "$2" ;;
    backup) rsync -a ~/data/ /mnt/$2/ ;;
    sync) git pull && git push ;;
    *) echo "Unknown command: $1" ;;
  esac
}

The code above is just a simplified example so you can get an idea of how it works. So, if I were to type kb backup external, it would have rsync send files from my data directory to the external hard drive I have mounted.

There are two reasons why I like having a dispatcher for all these aliases. First of all, I don't need to worry about collisions with actual commands. So, I can use words like deploy, backup, and sync, and since they're prefixed with "kb," they won't conflict with any similarly named commands in my system's PATH.

The other reason is that I can easily search for an alias that I'm having trouble remembering. Typing kb by itself pipes the list of subcommands into fzf (fuzzy search), so I have a searchable list of the aliases whenever I forget one. Here's what that looks like, placed right above the aforementioned case statement:

kb() {
  if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    local cmd
    cmd=$(printf "deploy
backup
sync
envreset
" | fzf --prompt="kb > ")
    [ -n "$cmd" ] && kb "$cmd"
    return
  fi
  
  # case statement
  
}

If an argument is not provided, it'll be caught by that function first, which gives me a list of aliases to choose from. I can pick the one I'm looking for, and it'll drop it right into the case statement below. Overkill? Probably, but it has saved me a surprising number of times.

Shortcuts are a double-edged sword

Try to remember the commands behind the aliases

After using my set of aliases and functions long enough, I find myself forgetting some of the actual commands they're meant to simplify. This is most evident when I'm on a new machine, and I start calling my custom aliases out of muscle memory, only to be met with an error in the Bash prompt. Sometimes, I have to think for a minute about how to type out the long sequence of commands I can usually recall in only a few keystrokes.

It's not a big concern, though, since all the aliases and functions are in a neatly organized plaintext file that I can easily consult at any time. It's not like I'm going to remember every Linux command all the time, anyway. Sometimes, it's helpful to have notes, and I just think of my .bash_shortcuts file as an extension of that.

Manually typing everything is too dang slow

Being able to type "kb" instead of 30 characters is a lot faster, but that's not the main reason I like it. I got tired of having to go through the same routine of executing three or four commands every time I was ready to do some work. Conjuring complex functions in mere seconds is like automating the most tedious part of using the terminal.

I feel that my Claude Pro subscription has been money well spent, given all the projects it has developed for me. There's only one recurring problem: the limited weekly usage sometimes isn't enough to finish a sizable codebase. Claude can certainly handle the complex projects. It's just a question of whether the usage capacity will let it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Last week, I gave Claude a huge task of coding a replacement for Google Sheets. I normally rely on Sonnet for development work, as it's much lighter on the tokens but still proves capable. For this project, though, I knew I'd need to resort to Opus. To extend my usage beyond what's normally possible, I told Opus to spawn Sonnet and Haiku sub-agents for the actual implementation work. This ended up being the perfect combo: it let me build a huge app while still leaving me usage to spare before the weekly reset.

I changed one setting in Claude Code, and my token burn dropped by 45%

Claude Code was overthinking the assignment

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I let Opus do the orchestration

And had lighter models do implementation

The secret to utilizing Opus without burning through usage credits in a matter of minutes is to limit the model strictly to the orchestration of the task. Then, it can delegate the actual implementation and testing to sub-agents running models like Sonnet and Haiku. Those models get their assignments from Opus, carry out the work, test it out, and report the results back to Opus.

Garmin is known mainly for its fitness wearables, but it also makes travel accessories too. Garmin Dash Cam Mini 3 features a 1080p camera with a 140-degree field of view, which can automatically save incidents that occur to a microSD card.

item.title: Windows 11's latest update makes 8GB PCs 20% more responsive, and multitasking up to 40% faster
item.itunes:title: Windows 11's latest update makes 8GB PCs 20% more responsive, and multitasking up to 40% faster
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The latest Windows 11 update makes 8GB PCs 20% more responsive and multitasking up to 40% faster.
  • Improved memory compression keeps up to 2GB more active data and cuts committed-memory growth up to 900MB.
  • Start, Search, File Explorer and Teams feel 20% faster; Teams enables Efficiency Mode by default on 8GB PCs.

After announcing plans to improve various aspects of Windows 11 a few months ago, including memory optimization for PCs with 8GB of RAM, Microsoft has kept its promise and released an update that does exactly that.

According to a blog post written by Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's EVP of Windows and Devices, the latest Windows 11 update (which should be available now) includes improvements that "make a real difference on PCs with 8GB of RAM." The tech giant outlines its approach in three parts: first, it wants to use memory better on every Windows 11 PC; next, it wants interactions to feel instant even under heavy load; and lastly, key apps will require less memory.

Overall, Microsoft says Windows 11 PCs will be 20% more responsive and multitasking up to 40% faster on PCs with 8GB of RAM. The company's blog post also explains how it tuned Windows 11's compression to work better on PCs with 8GB of RAM, allowing the OS to keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory.

Microsoft also outlines how key Windows 11 interactions feel faster, including opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, launching the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. Compared to Windows 11's January 2026 update, these features should feel 20% snappier, according to Microsoft. The OS accomplishes this by prioritizing what you're doing at that moment and pulling back on background tasks.

The efficiency improvements also extend to apps, though Microsoft only mentions Teams in its press release. It says Teams can turn on Efficiency Mode by default on 8GB PCs, allowing the app to launch 20% faster and use fewer system resources. The app can also adjust your laptop's camera resolution to free up processor capacity for audio, keeping your call clear when the PC is under a heavy load.

Microsoft performed extensive tests on Windows 11 PCs with 8GB of RAM

This update is part of the tech giant's broader plan to improve Windows 11

To round out its update announcement, Microsoft outlined a test in which an 8GB PC had 20 tabs open, including Microsoft Edge, a 4K video, a large Word document, PowerPoint, Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer, with everything open and running. According to the tech giant, a relatively intensive workflow like this will run 40% faster than it would on Windows 11's January 2026 build, with "reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900MB."

Moving forward, Microsoft's comprehensive plan to improve Windows 11 is still ongoing. The company says it plans to bring WinUI3 to more parts of Windows 11, including File Explorer, Notepad, Paint, Windows Search, and more, along with more improvements to memory compression and switching Search and Widgets to one web engine.

Microsoft's K2 Windows 11 improvement initiative has been ongoing for several months now. So far, we've seen CoPilot's integration rolled back, the taskbar moved to the top, bottom, left, or right, Windows Update's restart behavior making more sense, and Windows Search less cluttered and faster. Microsoft started talking more about Windows 11 memory efficiency after Apple released its $600 MacBook Neo, an A18 Pro-powered macOS laptop with just 8GB of RAM.

To download this update focused on performance and memory improvements, update to Windows 11, version 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later.
